claim: GSH is a tripeptide (glutamate–cysteine–glycine) essential for several cellular functions and the most prominent antioxidant in the brain.
source: GSH is a tripeptide (glutamate–cysteine–glycine) essential for several cellular functions and the most prominent antioxidant in the brain (Figure 1a; Rae and Williams, 2017; Zalachoras et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rae and Williams, 2017 and Zalachoras et al., 2020, and reference to Figure 1a showing GSH metabolic pathways.

claim: GSH plays a major role in the reduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: GSH plays a major role in the reduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Rae and Williams, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rae and Williams, 2017.

claim: ROS generation is coupled to energy production and cellular activity.
source: ROS generation is coupled to energy production and cellular activity (Cobley et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cobley et al., 2018.

claim: Effortful behavior engages the activation of the nucleus accumbens.
source: effortful behavior engages the activation of the NuAc (Schmidt et al., 2012; Pessiglione et al., 2007; Hailwood et al., 2018; Soares-Cunha et al., 2016; Soares-Cunha et al., 2018; Gallo et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies showing NuAc activation during effortful behavior.

claim: Altered GSH levels have been reported in the brain of patients in disorders that course along with motivational impairments.
source: altered GSH levels have been reported in the brain of patients in disorders that course along with motivational impairments (Lapidus et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lapidus et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: GSH levels in the nucleus accumbens show a positive correlation with successful 1 CHF trials in humans.
source: Indeed, GSH levels in NuAc (but not in the occipital lobe) show a positive correlation with successful 1 CHF - but not total - trials (Figure 1c, Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1c and 1d showing correlation between GSH and performance, with Spearman correlation ρ=0.52, p=0.01.

claim: Participants with higher accumbal GSH levels sustained their performance throughout the task, maintaining a similar number of successful 1 CHF trials in the first and second halves of the task.
source: A significant interaction in the high reward was observed (Figure 1e and f), indicating that H-GSH subjects sustained their performance throughout the task, maintaining a similar number of successful 1 CHF trials in the first and second halves of the task.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1e-f showing no significant difference between H1 and H2 for H-GSH group.

claim: Participants with low GSH levels showed a significant reduction in the number of successful trials in the second half of the task as compared to high GSH subjects.
source: In contrast, L-GSH subjects had a significant reduction in the number of successful trials in the second half of the task as compared to H-GSH subjects (Figure 1e–g).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1e-g showing L-GSH group had significantly fewer successful trials in H2 compared to H-GSH group (t(20) = −2.45, p=0.02).

claim: No significant correlations between GSH levels and performance were observed in the occipital cortex.
source: However, no significant correlations between GSH levels and performance were observed in the occipital cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—source data 1), considered here as a control brain region.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing no correlation (ρ=0.13, p=0.67) and Bayesian analysis (BF01=5.18).

claim: L-GSH rats spent more time immobile than H-GSH rats when tested in the forced swim test over a period of 15 min.
source: L-GSH rats spent more time immobile than H-GSH rats when tested in the FST over a period of 15 min (Figure 2e)
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2e showing significant difference (t(33) = 2.10, p=0.04).

claim: Differences in immobility between L-GSH and H-GSH rats particularly emerged on the second half of the forced swim test.
source: with differences particularly emerging on the second half of the task (Figure 2f).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2f showing significant time × GSH interaction (F(14, 504)=2.10, p=0.01).

claim: L-GSH and H-GSH rats did not show significant differences in anxiety-like behaviors.
source: The two groups did not differ in anxiety-like behaviors (Figure 2g).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2g showing no significant difference (t(33) = 0.85, p=0.40) and Bayesian analysis (BF01=2.30).

claim: H-GSH rats exhibited a higher breakpoint in the progressive ratio task than L-GSH rats.
source: However, in the increasing effort-based PR task, H-GSH rats exhibited a higher breakpoint (Figure 3e)
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3e showing significant difference (t(14) = 4.69, p<0.001).

claim: H-GSH rats obtained more rewards in the progressive ratio task than L-GSH rats.
source: obtained more rewards (Figure 3f)
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3f showing significant difference (t(14) = 2.84, p=0.01).

claim: H-GSH rats performed more correct nosepokes in the progressive ratio task than L-GSH rats.
source: and performed more correct nosepokes (Figure 3g) than L-GSH rats.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3g showing significant difference (t(14) = 2.66, p=0.02).

claim: The two groups did not significantly differ in the percentage of correct over total nosepokes.
source: Importantly, the two groups did not significantly differ in the percentage of correct over total (correct and incorrect) nosepokes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1g showing no significant difference.

claim: NuAc GSH levels were correlated with the number of rewards obtained during the PR task.
source: In addition to the effort-based reward-incentivized effects observed in the L- and H-GSH groups, NuAc GSH levels were correlated with the number of rewards obtained during the PR task (Figure 3—figure supplement 1l).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1l showing correlation (Pearson r=0.49, p=0.038).

claim: All animals readily consumed all pellets when given free access to 20 sucrose pellets, suggesting no group differences in appetite or in the perceived palatability of the pellets.
source: Finally, when subsets of H-GSH and L-GSH rats were allowed free access to 20 sucrose pellets (more than any rat managed to acquire during the time they were given access to the PR test), all animals readily consumed all pellets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1m), suggesting no group differences in appetite or in the perceived palatability of the pellets.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1m showing all animals consumed all pellets.

claim: No significant differences were found between H- and L-GSH rats in saccharine preference under basal conditions.
source: In addition, given the NuAc's involvement in reward processing and anhedonia (Berridge and Kringelbach, 2008), we examined whether there were differences in saccharine preference between H- and L-GSH rats under basal conditions but found no significant differences between groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1n).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1n showing no significant difference.

claim: BSO infusion into the nucleus accumbens was effective in reducing GSH levels.
source: Our BSO dose was effective in reducing GSH levels as verified via HPLC measurements (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4c showing significant reduction (t(32) = 2.15, p=0.039).

claim: BSO-infused animals achieved a lower breakpoint in the PR test than saline-infused animals.
source: In the PR test, BSO-infused animals achieved a lower breakpoint (Figure 4d)
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4d showing significant difference (t(38) = 2.64, p=0.012).

claim: BSO-infused animals obtained fewer rewards in the PR test than saline-infused animals.
source: obtained fewer rewards (Figure 4e)
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4e showing significant difference (t(38) = 2.72, p=0.01).

claim: BSO-treated rats performed fewer correct nosepokes compared to vehicle-treated rats.
source: and performed fewer correct nosepokes (Figure 4f) than the Sal group.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4f showing significant difference (t(38) = 2.38, p=0.023).

claim: BSO-treated rats showed a significantly lower number of correct nosepokes over time.
source: However, BSO-treated rats showed a significantly lower number of correct nosepokes over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1h showing significant effect of treatment (F(1, 38)=6.17, p=0.018).

claim: A positive correlation between GSH levels and rewards obtained during the task that was observed in control animals was not evident in animals infused with BSO in the NuAc.
source: Interestingly, a positive correlation between GSH levels and rewards obtained during the task that was observed in control animals was not evident in animals infused with BSO in the NuAc (Figure 4—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1i showing no correlation (Pearson r=–0.16, p=0.42) and Bayesian analysis (BF01=3.16).

claim: 4 weeks after BSO treatment, no decrease on the breakpoint reached was observed in BSO-treated rats.
source: Importantly, 4 weeks after BSO treatment, no decrease on the breakpoint reached was observed in BSO-treated rats (Figure 4h; BF01=4.08)
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4h showing no significant difference (t(32) = 0.47, p=0.64) and Bayesian analysis (BF01=4.08).

claim: No significant differences were observed in activated caspase 3 staining between Sal and BSO groups.
source: No significant staining differences were observed between Sal and BSO groups, indicating a lack of BSO toxicity at the dose used in this experiment.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1l-m showing no significant difference in caspase 3 activation.

claim: NAC treatment increased accumbal GSH levels in rats.
source: Here we confirmed its effectiveness to increase accumbal GSH levels in a separate cohort of animals (Figure 5c)
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5c showing significant increase (t(47) = 2.97, p=0.005).

claim: NAC-treated rats reached a higher breakpoint than vehicle-treated rats in the PR test.
source: NAC-treated rats performed better in the PR session than vehicle-treated rats, achieving a higher breakpoint (Figure 5d)
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5d showing significant difference (t(17) = 2.27, p=0.036).

claim: NAC-treated rats obtained more rewards than vehicle-treated rats in the PR test.
source: obtaining more rewards (Figure 5e)
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5e showing significant difference (t(17) = 2.21, p=0.041).

claim: NAC treatment did not affect intrinsic excitability of MSNs.
source: No significant differences were observed in passive cell properties, spiking threshold, and firing frequency when cells were depolarized by somatic current injections (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a-d), indicating that NAC treatment did not affect intrinsic excitability of MSNs.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a-d showing no significant differences in cell properties.

claim: mEPSCs recorded in D1-MSNs exhibited significantly larger peak amplitudes in NAC-treated rats.
source: Miniature postsynaptic excitatory currents (mEPSCs) recorded in D1-MSNs exhibited significantly larger peak amplitudes in NAC-treated rats, with no significant differences in the inter-event interval (Figure 6d).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6d showing significant difference in cumulative frequency (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, D=0.16, p<0.001).

claim: mEPSC peak amplitudes were significantly reduced in D2-MSNs in NAC-treated rats.
source: By contrast, mEPSC peak amplitudes were significantly reduced in D2-MSNs, and were also less frequent, as indicated by the pronounced increase in the inter-event interval (Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6e showing significant differences in cumulative frequency for both peak amplitude (D=0.075, p<0.001) and inter-event interval (D=0.22, p<0.001).

claim: The weight of glutamatergic synaptic drive in the NuAc core is altered by NAC treatment, such that D1-MSNs receive larger excitatory inputs, while these are overall reduced in D2-MSNs.
source: Overall, these data indicate that the weight of glutamatergic synaptic drive in the NuAc core is altered by the NAC treatment, such that D1-MSNs receive larger excitatory inputs, while these are overall reduced in D2-MSNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing differential effects on D1- and D2-MSNs.

claim: The resulting augmented engagement of D1-MSNs over D2-MSNs is consistent with the purported roles of the two cell types in approach/avoidance behavior, thus offering a plausible cellular substrate for the enhanced performance in the PR task.
source: The resulting augmented engagement of D1-MSNs over D2-MSNs is consistent with the purported roles of the two cell types in approach/avoidance behavior, thus offering a plausible cellular substrate for the enhanced performance in the PR task.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the electrophysiological findings to behavioral outcomes based on established knowledge about D1- and D2-MSN functions.

claim: Higher accumbal GSH levels are highly predictive of better, and particularly, steady performance over time in effort-related tasks.
source: Using proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy at ultra-high field in both male humans and rodent populations, we establish that higher accumbal GSH levels are highly predictive of better, and particularly, steady performance over time in effort-related tasks.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined human and rodent data showing correlations and causal relationships between GSH and performance.

claim: Downregulating GSH levels through micro-injections of the GSH synthesis inhibitor buthionine sulfoximine in the nucleus accumbens impaired effort-based reward-incentivized performance.
source: Causality was established in in vivo experiments in rats that, first, showed that downregulating GSH levels through micro-injections of the GSH synthesis inhibitor buthionine sulfoximine in the nucleus accumbens impaired effort-based reward-incentivized performance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing BSO infusion reduced GSH and impaired PR performance.

claim: Systemic treatment with the GSH precursor N-acetyl-cysteine increased accumbal GSH levels in rats and led to improved performance.
source: In addition, systemic treatment with the GSH precursor N-acetyl-cysteine increased accumbal GSH levels in rats and led to improved performance, potentially mediated by a cell-type-specific shift in glutamatergic inputs to accumbal medium spiny neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing NAC treatment increased GSH and improved PR performance.

claim: Improvement of accumbal antioxidant function may be a feasible approach to boost motivation.
source: They also suggest that improvement of accumbal antioxidant function may be a feasible approach to boost motivation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the NAC treatment results.

claim: The nucleus accumbens is a critical node of the brain's reward and motivation circuitries.
source: A great deal of work in both rodents and humans highlights the nucleus accumbens (NuAc) - a main component of the ventral striatum - as a critical node of the brain's reward and motivation circuitries (Pessiglione et al., 2018; Salamone et al., 2007; Croxson et al., 2009; Haber, 2011; Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Incentives energize effortful behavior through the recruitment of the nucleus accumbens.
source: Indeed, incentives energize effortful behavior (Berchio et al., 2019; Robinson et al., 2014) through the recruitment of the NuAc (Schmidt et al., 2012; Knutson et al., 2001; Pessiglione et al., 2007; Hailwood et al., 2018; Soares-Cunha et al., 2016; Soares-Cunha et al., 2018; Gallo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Alterations in NuAc function are implicated in psychopathological conditions that involve motivational deficits, such as depression.
source: Moreover, alterations in NuAc function are implicated in psychopathological conditions that involve motivational deficits, such as depression (Epstein et al., 2006; Hanson et al., 2015; Muir et al., 2019; Treadway et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Accumbal mitochondrial function and metabolism play a key role in the regulation of motivated behavior.
source: Emerging evidence underscores a key role for accumbal mitochondrial function and metabolism in the regulation of motivated behavior (Hollis et al., 2015; van der Kooij et al., 2018a; Strasser et al., 2020; Gebara et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Glutamine levels, and particularly, an increased glutamine-to-glutamate ratio in the NuAc predict both, a higher performance related to task endurance and a lower effort perception in a physical effort-based motivated task.
source: Recent work in humans using proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) focusing on the components of the glutamate/GABA-glutamine cycle has shown that glutamine levels, and particularly, an increased glutamine-to-glutamate ratio in the NuAc predict both, a higher performance related to task endurance and a lower effort perception in a physical effort-based motivated task (Strasser et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Strasser et al., 2020.

claim: Glutamine is the main precursor for the synthesis of glutamate.
source: Glutamine is the main precursor for the synthesis of glutamate (Walls et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Walls et al., 2015.

claim: Glutamate is a building block for the production of glutathione.
source: a building block for the production of glutathione (GSH; Forman et al., 2009; Sappington et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Forman et al., 2009 and Sappington et al., 2016.

claim: The CRLB for GSH in human 1H-MRS measurements was 8.2 ± 2.8%.
source: The Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) for GSH was 8.2 ± 2.8%.
evidence: This is a technical measurement parameter reported from the human MRS study.

claim: NAC is a donor of cysteine (the rate-limiting substrate for GSH synthesis).
source: N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC) is a donor of Cys (the rate-limiting substrate)
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1a schematic.

claim: BSO is a specific inhibitor of γ-GCS (gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase).
source: buthionine sulfoximine (BSO) is a specific inhibitor of γ-GCS.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1a schematic.

claim: γ-GCS is the rate-limiting enzyme for GSH synthesis.
source: It is synthesized in the cytosol by an ATP-dependent two-step process catalyzed by γ-glutamyl cysteine synthase/ligase (γ-GCS) and GSH synthetase (GSS), with γ-GCS as the rate-limiting enzyme.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: GSH can exist in a reduced (GSH) or in an oxidized (GSSG) state.
source: GSH or γ-L-glutamyl-L-cysteinylglycine, is a tripeptide, that can exist in a reduced (GSH) or in an oxidized (Glutathione disulfide, GSSG) state.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The nucleus accumbens is incrementally recruited as the expected reward increases.
source: Indeed, human studies have shown that the NuAc (or the ventral striatum more broadly) is the main brain structure to respond to incentives (Schmidt et al., 2012; Knutson et al., 2001; O'Doherty et al., 2004; Yacubian et al., 2006) being incrementally recruited as the expected reward increases (Knutson et al., 2001; Sescousse et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to human neuroimaging studies.

claim: NuAc activity relates to effort-based cost-benefit valuation.
source: NuAc activity relates to effort-based cost-benefit valuation (Croxson et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Croxson et al., 2009.

claim: Animals with higher breakpoints showed a greater magnitude of the NuAc O2 responses.
source: Animals with higher breakpoints showed a greater magnitude of the NuAc O2 responses, suggesting that individual differences in the capacity to remain on task for longer are related to the magnitude of O2 responses in the NuAc (Hailwood et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hailwood et al., 2018.

claim: The main O2-consuming cells in the brain are neurons.
source: Given that the main O2-consuming cells in the brain are neurons (Hall et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hall et al., 2012.

claim: Higher mitochondrial oxygen respiratory capacity in the NuAc in rodents has been shown to positively relate to the duration of active coping/escaping responses in the FST.
source: Importantly, higher mitochondrial oxygen respiratory capacity in the NuAc in rodents has been shown to positively relate to the duration of active coping/escaping responses in the FST (Gebara et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gebara et al., 2021.

claim: Higher mitochondrial oxygen respiratory capacity in the NuAc in rodents has been shown to positively relate to winning a social competition.
source: and to winning a social competition (Hollis et al., 2015; van der Kooij et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hollis et al., 2015 and van der Kooij et al., 2018a.

claim: GSH is the major antioxidant as well as a redox and cell-signaling regulator.
source: GSH is the major antioxidant as well as a redox and cell-signaling regulator (Rae and Williams, 2017; Dringen, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rae and Williams, 2017 and Dringen, 2000.

claim: The brain is highly susceptible to oxidative stress.
source: Given the high susceptibility of the brain to oxidative stress (Cobley et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cobley et al., 2018.

claim: Neurons require high levels of GSH to counteract oxidative stress and sustain cellular integrity and circuit function.
source: neurons require high levels of GSH to counteract oxidative stress and sustain cellular integrity and circuit function (Fernandez-Fernandez et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fernandez-Fernandez et al., 2018.

claim: GSH may be a physiological reservoir of glutamate neurotransmitter when the glutamate-glutamine shuttle is inhibited.
source: and recent evidence indicating that GSH may be a physiological reservoir of glutamate neurotransmitter when the glutamate-glutamine shuttle is inhibited (Sedlak et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sedlak et al., 2019.

claim: Systemic NAC treatment is efficient in targeting antioxidant levels in the ventral striatum.
source: Our administration regime effectively increased accumbal GSH content, supporting the efficiency of systemic NAC treatment in targeting antioxidant levels in the ventral striatum.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing NAC increased accumbal GSH.

claim: Selective activation of specific glutamatergic inputs to the NuAc has been shown to promote reward-based motivation.
source: Selective activation of specific glutamatergic inputs to the NuAc has been shown to promote reward-based motivation (Stuber et al., 2008; Day et al., 2007; Flagel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stuber et al., 2008, Day et al., 2007, and Flagel et al., 2011.

claim: Prolonged systemic treatment with NAC induces cell-subtype-specific changes in synaptic transmission in the NuAc core.
source: Hence, we provide novel evidence that prolonged systemic treatment with NAC induces cell-subtype-specific changes in synaptic transmission in the NuAc core
evidence: Supported by the electrophysiological data showing differential effects on D1- and D2-MSNs.

claim: In NAC-treated rats, excitatory inputs promote activation of D1-MSNs over D2-MSNs as a result of the increased postsynaptic responses in D1-MSNs as well as the concomitant reduction in collateral inhibition provided by D2-MSNs.
source: This suggests that, in NAC-treated rats, excitatory inputs promote activation of D1-MSNs over D2-MSNs as a result of the increased postsynaptic responses in D1-MSNs as well as the concomitant reduction in collateral inhibition provided by D2-MSNs (Ducrocq et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data and cited literature on D2-MSN collateral inhibition.

claim: The shift toward D1-MSN activation is expected to support motivated behavior, according to the canonical roles of D1- and D2-MSNs in positive reinforcement and aversion, respectively.
source: The shift toward D1-MSN activation is expected to support motivated behavior, according to the canonical roles of D1- and D2-MSNs in positive reinforcement and aversion, respectively (Kravitz et al., 2012; Lobo et al., 2010; Floresco, 2015)
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about D1- and D2-MSN functions, supported by citations.

claim: Cystine derived from NAC binds the cystine-glutamate exchanger in glial cells and shifts the extracellular levels of glutamate.
source: In addition to promoting GSH synthesis, cystine derived from NAC also binds the cystine-glutamate exchanger in glial cells and shifts the extracellular levels of glutamate (Tardiolo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tardiolo et al., 2018.

claim: Alterations in the metabolic pathways leading to the synthesis of GSH can affect glutamate levels and accumulation.
source: Moreover, alterations in the metabolic pathways leading to the synthesis of GSH can affect glutamate levels and accumulation (Koga et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Koga et al., 2011.

claim: Glutamate activity can be shaped by GSH.
source: and glutamate activity can also be shaped by GSH (Sedlak et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sedlak et al., 2019.

claim: Opposite effects on glutamatergic transmission have been shown to occur in D1- and D2-MSNs upon drug exposure.
source: Notably, opposite effects on glutamatergic transmission have been shown to occur in D1- and D2-MSNs upon drug exposure (Zinsmaier et al., 2022), confirming that synaptic adaptations in the NuAc can take place in a cell-type-specific manner.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zinsmaier et al., 2022.

claim: NAC interventions have been applied in animal models of addiction and have proven successful in rescuing drug-seeking behavior by normalizing extracellular glutamate levels.
source: NAC interventions have been applied in animal models of addiction and have proven successful in rescuing drug-seeking behavior by normalizing extracellular glutamate levels, thereby modulating accumbal excitatory transmission via metabotropic receptors (Olive et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olive et al., 2012.

claim: Intra-individual variation in GSH content seems to be rather stable over time.
source: Importantly, as shown in some cell types, intra-individual variation in GSH content seems to be rather stable over time (van 't Erve et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to van 't Erve et al., 2013.

claim: Individual capacity to produce GSH is determined by genetic variability in enzymes involved in its production and/or regeneration.
source: Individual capacity to produce GSH is determined by genetic variability in enzymes involved in its production and/or regeneration, including several common single nucleotide polymorphisms that regulate GSH levels and associated processes (Dasari et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dasari et al., 2018.

claim: Several life conditions can affect brain GSH levels, particularly under situations leading to increased ROS expression and oxidative stress such as during ageing or psychogenic stress.
source: In addition, several life conditions can also affect brain GSH levels, particularly under situations leading to increased ROS expression and oxidative stress such as during ageing or psychogenic stress (Zalachoras et al., 2020; Sohal et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zalachoras et al., 2020 and Sohal et al., 1994.

claim: Several psychopathological alterations - such as depression or schizophrenia - in which low GSH levels have been reported are associated with motivational deficits or fatigue.
source: Accordingly, several psychopathological alterations - such as depression or schizophrenia - in which low GSH levels have been reported are associated with motivational deficits or fatigue (Lapidus et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019; Xin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lapidus et al., 2014, Wang et al., 2019, and Xin et al., 2016.

claim: Nutritional treatments leading to 15–20% change in accumbal GSH content are able to modulate motivated performance in healthy individuals.
source: Moreover, we provide a proof of principle that nutritional treatments leading to 15–20% change in accumbal GSH content are able to modulate motivated performance in healthy individuals.
evidence: This is a summary of the NAC treatment findings showing approximately 15-20% increase in GSH (from Figure 5c data) and improved performance.

claim: GSH levels in the NuAc are both a predictive marker of differences in reward-based effortful performance and a potential target for nutritional or other type of interventions.
source: In conclusion, we establish GSH levels in the NuAc both as a predictive marker of differences in reward-based effortful performance and as a potential target for nutritional or other type of interventions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined correlational and causal findings.

claim: Chronic NAC supplementation has promising potential to boost accumbal GSH levels and to regulate motivation to exert reward-incentivized effort.
source: We also provide strong evidence for a promising potential of chronic NAC supplementation to boost accumbal GSH levels and to regulate motivation to exert reward-incentivized effort.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the NAC treatment findings.

claim: The studies were performed in male humans and rodents.
source: However, it is important to note that our sample sizes are relatively small, and thus the absence of significant effects should be interpreted with caution. As our studies were performed in male humans and rodents, it is important to note as a limitation to our findings.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a limitation.

claim: The sample sizes in the study are relatively small.
source: However, it is important to note that our sample sizes are relatively small, and thus the absence of significant effects should be interpreted with caution.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a limitation.

claim: NAC is a cysteine precursor that has been documented to increase GSH levels in the brain.
source: Finally, aiming at a translational application, we evaluated the efficiency of nutritional supplementation with N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC) - a cysteine precursor that has been documented to increase GSH levels in the brain (Zalachoras et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zalachoras et al., 2020.

claim: The nucleus accumbens core appears to guide goal-directed behavior toward the reward, whereas the shell inhibits goal-irrelevant behavior by avoiding irrelevant, non-rewarded, or less preferable outcome.
source: In addition, although both core and shell division of the NuAc contribute to motivated behavior, such as performance in the PR task, the core appears to guide goal-directed behavior toward the reward, whereas the shell inhibits goal-irrelevant behavior by avoiding irrelevant, non-rewarded, or less preferable outcome (Floresco, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Floresco, 2015.

claim: The two main NuAc neuronal populations are medium spiny neurons expressing the dopamine receptor type 1 (D1-MSNs) and type 2 (D2-MSNs).
source: The two main NuAc neuronal populations [i.e. medium spiny neurons (MSNs) expressing the dopamine receptor type 1 (D1-MSNs) and type 2 (D2-MSNs)]
evidence: This is established knowledge about NuAc cell types.

claim: D1-MSNs and D2-MSNs are classically described as mediators of distinct types of behavior (e.g. approach versus avoidance).
source: The two main NuAc neuronal populations [i.e. medium spiny neurons (MSNs) expressing the dopamine receptor type 1 (D1-MSNs) and type 2 (D2-MSNs)] are classically described as mediators of distinct types of behavior (e.g. approach versus avoidance; Kravitz et al., 2012; Lobo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kravitz et al., 2012 and Lobo et al., 2010.

claim: Valid NuAc 1H-MRS and behavioral data were obtained from 22 participants in the human study.
source: Valid NuAc 1H-MRS and behavioral data were obtained from 22 participants (more experimental details can be found in the Participants section in Supplementary methods of ref Strasser et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the human study sample.

claim: The NuAc region of interest voxel was defined by the third ventricle medially, the subcallosal area inferiorly, and the body of the caudate nucleus and the putamen laterally and superiorly.
source: The NuAc region of interest voxel was defined by the third ventricle medially, the subcallosal area inferiorly, and the body of the caudate nucleus and the putamen laterally and superiorly, in line with definitions of NuAc anatomy identifiable on MRIs (Smith et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the human MRS acquisition, supported by citation to Smith et al., 2002.

claim: Adult male Wistar rats weighing 250–275 g upon arrival were used in the study.
source: Adult male Wistar rats (Charles Rivers, Saint-German-Nuelle, France) weighing 250–275 g upon arrival were individually housed with ad libitum access to food and water in a 12 light-dark cycle (lights switched on at 7:00 am) and a constant temperature at 22 ± 2°C.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the animal subjects.
